planting.note: Plant offsets in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun to light shade; give some afternoon shade in hot inland climates to preserve leaf color.

directions: This low, stemless Madagascar species forms a tight rosette of firm, dull green to grayish leaves marked with irregular pale spots, most pronounced on young growth. The leaf margins carry small, closely spaced, triangular reddish teeth that give the species its epithet. It offsets slowly to form modest clusters and sends up slender spikes of coral to salmon flowers in winter. It is more compact and slower to clump than the widely grown Aloe maculata, and its spotting is finer and more irregular than that species' bold blotches.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant offsets in well-drained soil in full sun; the strongest orange-red color develops under bright light and lean, somewhat stressed conditions.

directions: Native to Tanzania's Usambara Mountains, this small stoloniferous species produces low rosettes of narrow, tapering leaves lined with fine white marginal teeth. In full sun and lean soil the foliage shifts from green to a saturated orange-red to coppery hue, the trait behind its common name; plants kept in shade or rich soil stay mostly green. It spreads by runners to form loose colonies over time and blooms with slim spikes of yellow-orange flowers. Its color intensity in sun distinguishes it from the similarly small Aloe humilis, which stays blue-gray rather than flushing red.

planting.note: Plant offsets in a shallow container or rock-garden pocket with fast-draining mix in bright light; this dwarf form is well suited to small pots and windowsill growing.

directions: A selection of the miniature Madagascar species Aloe rauhii, 'Snowflake' forms tiny rosettes only a few inches across, densely covered in small white flecks that give the foliage a frosted, speckled look against soft green leaves. It offsets freely at the base to build a tight mounding cluster and produces small spikes of orange flowers on thin stalks well above the foliage. Because of its small scale and heavy spotting it is a popular parent in dwarf hybrid aloe breeding and a common choice for terrariums and dish gardens rather than open garden beds. It stays noticeably smaller than Aloe haworthioides, another miniature species, and lacks that species' soft marginal bristles.

planting.note: Plant at the base of a fence, shrub, or trellis in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; the lax stems need something to scramble through or over to display their form.

directions: Unlike most aloes, this South African species does not form a single ground-level rosette; instead it produces slender, sprawling stems set with narrow, lax leaves that scramble and climb through neighboring shrubbery, reaching considerable length where supported and often billed as one of the few true climbing succulents. Loose whorls of leaves occur along the stem rather than one basal cluster, and it flowers freely and repeatedly through the year with small clusters of scarlet-orange, bicolor-tipped blooms that draw hummingbirds and sunbirds. Left unsupported it sprawls as a loose groundcover mound instead of climbing. Its scrambling, multi-stemmed habit readily distinguishes it from rosette-forming species like Aloe arborescens or Aloe maculata.

planting.note: Plant in a shallow, very fast-draining mineral mix in full sun; this Namib-adjacent species is extremely rot-prone and should be watered sparingly, mainly during active summer growth.

directions: Native to rocky ground along the edge of Namibia's Namib Desert, this nearly stemless species packs its stiff, gray-green leaves into a tight, ball-like rosette rather than the open, spreading form typical of most aloes. Each leaf curves inward and is armed along the margin with closely set white teeth, giving the whole plant a spiny, hedgehog-like silhouette. Growth is extremely slow and the plant stays small and solitary for years before offsetting sparingly. Its tight globe form and dense marginal spines set it apart from the similarly compact but open-rosetted Aloe brevifolia and from the softer-spined Aloe humilis.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant young specimens in a raised, sharply drained bed in full sun; this critically endangered Richtersveld species is extremely slow-growing and best sited where it can develop undisturbed for decades.

directions: Found only along the arid Richtersveld border of South Africa and Namibia, this is one of the largest tree-forming aloes, developing a thick, sparsely branched trunk topped with small rosettes of gray-green leaves relative to its overall bulk. It is close kin to the quiver tree, Aloe dichotoma, but grows taller, branches less, and holds its leaf rosettes at the tips of far fewer, thicker limbs, giving mature plants a stark, wind-sculpted silhouette. Wild populations are critically endangered and reproduce very slowly, so plants in cultivation are almost always nursery-grown from seed. Growth is exceptionally slow even in ideal garden conditions, with decades needed to approach anything like its wild stature.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with room to develop a branching trunk over time; give young plants some protection from hard frost until established.

directions: Endemic to Madagascar, this large tree aloe develops a stout trunk that branches near the base into several thick stems, each topped with a dense rosette of broad, blue-green leaves. Mature plants produce tall, showy spikes of deep red flowers in winter, held well above the foliage in a display that has made it a popular landscape specimen in mild, frost-free climates. It grows considerably faster and bulks up sooner than the slower South African tree aloes such as Aloe barberae, though it still takes years to develop its full branching, candelabra-like form. Its blue-green leaf color and dense basal branching distinguish it from the single-trunked Aloe barberae and from the more open-branching Aloe dichotoma.

planting.note: Plant offsets or divisions in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this vigorous species tolerates a wider range of garden conditions than many aloes and is often used as a xeric groundcover.

directions: Native to the highlands of Eritrea and Ethiopia, this vigorous, clump-forming species produces broad, fleshy green leaves in medium-sized rosettes that offset readily to form dense colonies. Tall, branched spikes of yellow-orange to greenish-yellow flowers rise well above the foliage in late winter and early spring, making it one of the showier bloomers among the mid-sized landscape aloes. It is more cold-tolerant and adaptable to garden soil than many South African species, which has made it a common xeriscape planting in frost-free and near-frost-free regions. Its plain green, unspotted leaves and rapid clumping habit distinguish it from the similarly sized but heavily spotted Aloe maculata.

planting.note: Plant in a gritty, mineral, fast-draining mix in full sun; this Namaqualand species needs sharp drainage and minimal summer water to avoid rot.

directions: Found along the arid Richtersveld and Namaqualand border of South Africa and Namibia, this slow-growing, usually solitary species carries stiff, blue-gray leaves edged and often surfaced with hard, prominent teeth that darken to near black with age, creating a striking contrast against the pale foliage. Older plants may develop a short stem as lower leaves die back, but the rosette otherwise stays compact and dense. It blooms in summer with spikes of red to orange flowers. The dark, heavily armed leaf margins are more pronounced than in the related Aloe krapohliana, making the two easy to tell apart once teeth color is visible.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
